cf.title: POC: PLpgSQL FOREACH IN JSON ARRAY

input.subject: POC: PLpgSQL FOREACH IN JSON ARRAY

verdict_reasoning: Two committers asked for a generic mechanism and did not question the goal, so the demand objections do not stop review at level 1b. The design is not yet agreed. Tom Lane's concern in message #20 that the iterator should not know the target type has no reply after the options struct (maintenance-fit-1). The author also leaves the casting default open (maintenance-fit-2), and nobody discussed putting by-name binding under IN ARRAY (standards-compat-3).

brief.title: PL/pgSQL foreach loop over jsonb arrays via subscripting iterator API
brief.problem: PL/pgSQL code that loops over JSON array elements today uses FOR IN SELECT over jsonb_array_elements, which runs the SQL executor for each loop. The author wants a faster and more readable loop for PL/pgSQL authors who process JSON arrays.
brief.proposed_design: The first version added new syntax FOREACH target IN JSON ARRAY expr. After Peter Eisentraut and Tom Lane asked for a generic mechanism, the patch now extends SubscriptRoutines with an optional iterator constructor, implements it for arrays and jsonb, and lets the existing FOREACH ... IN ARRAY accept a jsonb expression. JSON object fields go to a composite variable or a list of variables by name, and the iterator takes an optional target type and coercion mode.
user_visible_surface: FOREACH target IN ARRAY now accepts a jsonb expression; the earlier IN JSON ARRAY syntax is gone from the latest patch.
Object elements are assigned to a composite target or a variable list by field name, not by position.
SLICE greater than zero is rejected for jsonb arrays; a RECORD target needs a known structure first.
C API: SubscriptRoutines gets an optional iterator constructor, with options for result type and an ForeachAIteratorMode enum.
Error messages from existing FOREACH IN ARRAY cases may change, as Tom Lane said was acceptable.
author_claims: The loop is about 3 to 4 times faster than FOR IN SELECT over jsonb_array_elements, best case on a 1000-element array.
Jim Jones reported about 3 times faster in his own test.
The feature is new and has no compatibility issues.
The iterator must know the target type to do jsonb-to-composite conversion and to avoid I/O casts.
Splitting iterate and coerce into separate callbacks makes scalar loops about 2 times slower, slower than FOR IN SELECT.
brief.thread_state: Tom Lane questioned whether the iterator should know the target type and benchmarked a separate coerce() callback; Pavel answered with an options struct, now passed to the constructor. Nobody has replied to the last two versions, and the entry is in Needs review after a Ready for Committer status was reverted.
unclear: The proposal does not decide between strict and lax casting, nor whether ERROR ON ERROR style clauses will exist.
Which ForeachAIteratorMode values PL/pgSQL uses, and which modes jsonb and array iterators support.
No user other than PL/pgSQL is named for the iterator API, so the need for a general facility is untested.
The patch does not say whether plain json, as opposed to jsonb, input is accepted in the new form.
The thread does not show whether Tom Lane accepts target-type knowledge inside the iterator.

prior_attempts.title: iteration over record in plpgsql
prior_attempts.quote: While I don't have a problem with hstore_to_array, I don't think that row_to_array is a very good idea; it's basically encouraging people to throw away SQL datatypes altogether and imagine that everything is text.
prior_attempts.reason: Tom Lane objected that row_to_array casts all fields to text and drops SQL datatypes, and said row_to_json already covers the case. He also asked that the two features be split and that FOREACH get its own discussion. Jim Nasby worried that the FOREACH pairing rule would block iteration that follows array dimensions. The later messages move to typed iteration over records and broader dynamic typing, and no revised design was agreed.
prior_attempts.what_is_different: P1 extended FOREACH with a key/value variable list over a row turned into a text array. This proposal assigns jsonb object fields by name to typed targets with coercion, so it does not reduce values to text.

objections.title: Iterator API in SubscriptRoutines is still shaped for PL/pgSQL
objections.failure_scenario: An extension author adds iteration to a subscriptable type such as hstore. The constructor takes a target type and a five-value ForeachAIteratorMode, so the author must write coercion and composite conversion logic that only PL/pgSQL defines. Each type's iterator then casts slightly differently, and users find out when the same FOREACH behaves differently per type.
objections.argument: In message #20, Tom Lane said the point of using SubscriptRoutines is a general facility, and that iterators probably should not know the target type. The v20260803 patch still passes the result type and a coercion mode to the constructor (messages #26, #28), and PL/pgSQL remains the only caller. Message #25 says a separate coerce step is slower than FOR IN SELECT, but its own table shows the int case at about 48 ms against about 61 ms for FOR IN SELECT. A cleaner API would still be faster than today's FOR IN SELECT loop.
objections.author_must_show: Which ForeachAIteratorMode values must every iterator support, and why can coercion not stay in PL/pgSQL, given that the coerce-callback numbers still beat FOR IN SELECT?

critic.reasoning: Tom Lane's concern in message #20 has no reply after the options struct in messages #26 to #28. The speed claim holds only for int, since the numeric case in the same mode takes about 72 ms against 61 ms for FOR IN SELECT.

objections.title: Casting defaults fixed under old syntax before strict or lax is decided
objections.failure_scenario: A release ships FOREACH x IN ARRAY jsonb_expr with the current mixed rule, where 3.14 casts to int but "3.14" fails. Users write functions that rely on this. A later release that adds lax mode or ERROR ON ERROR clauses cannot change the default without silently changing how those functions behave.
objections.argument: Messages #1 and #28 and the latest commit message leave the strict-versus-lax question open and invite discussion, but nobody in the thread has answered it. Message #21 shows that plain assignment from jsonb and FOREACH conversion already follow different rules. Reusing the existing IN ARRAY keyword means the default casting behaviour is part of a long-lived language contract, so it should be settled before commit and not after.
objections.author_must_show: Which casting default is proposed for jsonb elements, and how would later ERROR ON ERROR clauses be added without changing what existing functions do?

critic.reasoning: The latest commit message states a preference for the old strict behaviour but still presents the choice as an open question, and no reviewer answered it. Optional clauses could be added later over a strict default, so this stays fixable.

objections.title: IN ARRAY becomes the spelling for any subscriptable type
objections.failure_scenario: An extension type such as hstore adds the new iterator, and FOREACH k IN ARRAY h starts to loop over a value that is not an array, with its own target-binding and slicing rules. Readers of the function cannot tell from the statement whether the loop binds by position or by name.
objections.argument: The docs already say other FOREACH variants for non-array composites "may be added in future", which suggests a separate keyword. The latest patch drops IN JSON ARRAY and puts jsonb under IN ARRAY, though jsonb loops bind by name and reject SLICE > 0. Message #13 backs a generic iterator, but the thread has not settled the user-facing spelling.
objections.author_must_show: Why should non-array subscriptable types share the IN ARRAY spelling instead of a distinct FOREACH variant, given that their binding rules differ?

critic.reasoning: Message #13 supports a generic iterator but says nothing about the user-facing keyword. The hstore case is hypothetical, but for jsonb alone the latest patch already puts by-name binding and a SLICE restriction under IN ARRAY without discussion.

objections.title: JSON keys bind to local variable names, and misses become NULLs
objections.failure_scenario: A developer renames local variables x, y to v_x, v_y in a function that uses FOREACH x, y IN ARRAY. The loop still runs, but no key matches, so every iteration assigns NULL to both variables. Nobody sees a problem until wrong data shows up downstream.
objections.argument: The documentation hunk shows that missing keys give NULL with no error, as in the '{}' row. Local variable names are internal to PL/pgSQL today. This rule makes them part of the data contract, which no other PL/pgSQL target list does, since arrays and composites bind by position. Whether a missing key should raise an error belongs to the undecided strict and lax question.
objections.author_must_show: What stops a variable rename from turning every value into NULL, and why is no error raised when no key matches any target variable?

critic.reasoning: Message #1 explains why binding is by name, and jsonb_populate_record also gives NULL for missing keys. But the thread does not discuss a variable list where no key matches, and the rename scenario is concrete.

objections.title: Benchmarks skip the existing idiom of building an array once, then FOREACH
objections.failure_scenario: A PL/pgSQL author who needs a fast loop over a jsonb array can already write `foreach x in array array(select jsonb_array_elements_text($1)::int)`, or array_agg over jsonb_populate_recordset for objects. That runs the executor once, not per row. If this idiom is close in speed, core carries a new iterator API in SubscriptRoutines and new FOREACH semantics for a small gain.
objections.argument: Every speed figure in the thread compares the patch only with FOR IN SELECT over jsonb_array_elements (message #1, #4, #25). The materialize-then-FOREACH idiom uses only existing features, and message #25 shows FOREACH over a ready array at about 11 ms against 25 ms for the patch. Name-based mapping of objects to a composite also exists already through jsonb_populate_recordset and jsonb_to_recordset. So the measured gain over the best existing approach is unknown, and so is the readability gain.
objections.author_must_show: How does the patch compare with FOREACH over an array built once by array(select jsonb_array_elements...) or array_agg over jsonb_populate_recordset, for scalars and composites?

critic.reasoning: Every figure in the thread compares only with FOR IN SELECT, and the array-built-once idiom can do the job for scalars and composites. The 11 ms control excludes the cost of building the array, so the real gap is unknown in both directions.

other_surviving.title: Speedup shown only for empty loop bodies, with no production workload
other_surviving.failure_scenario: A user changes a FOR IN SELECT jsonb_array_elements loop to FOREACH IN ARRAY because the release notes promise 3 to 4 times faster. The loop body runs an INSERT or UPDATE per element. The function runs at about the same speed, and the user also has to adapt to different cast behaviour.
other_surviving.argument: The benchmarks in message #25 time loops that only sum values: 100k int elements take about 25 ms with the patch against 60 ms with FOR IN SELECT, so about 0.35 µs is saved per element. Any SQL statement in the loop body costs more than that, so the gain matters only for loops whose body is pure PL/pgSQL. The thread names no user, -general report or production function where this loop overhead is the bottleneck, and FOR IN SELECT already works. Messages #11 and #13 accept the idea in principle but give no demand evidence.
other_surviving.author_must_show: Which real PL/pgSQL functions spend a measurable share of their run time in jsonb array loop overhead, and how much faster do they get with this patch?

critic.reasoning: The thread shows no field report, though two committers discussed how to build the feature and did not question whether to build it. The per-element figure comes from 100k-element arrays and may understate the gain for short arrays, as message #25 suggests.

refuted.title: Default cast behaviour for jsonb elements is undecided but fixed once shipped
refuted.failure_scenario: A release ships FOREACH over jsonb with today's strict casting, and functions start to depend on errors for values like "3.14" in an int loop. A later release adds ERROR ON ERROR clauses or a lax default to match SQL/JSON. Either the default stays strict for good, or existing functions start returning NULLs after upgrade without warning.
refuted.argument: Message #1 and both commit messages leave strict versus lax open, and the commit message sketches ERROR ON EMPTY ERROR ON ERROR clauses that do not exist yet. SQL/JSON functions are lax by default, but the patch picks the older strict json-function behaviour because the loop reuses IN ARRAY syntax. Once the behaviour ships, the default cannot change without breaking callers. The thread has not settled this.
refuted.author_must_show: Which default, strict or lax, will FOREACH over jsonb keep permanently, and how will a later ON ERROR clause fit without changing behaviour for existing functions?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of maintenance-fit-2, which describes the current rule more exactly as mixed (3.14 casts to int, "3.14" fails) and cites message #21.

touch_points.label: ABI / extension API
touch_points.reason: SubscriptRoutines in subscripting.h gets an optional iterator constructor with a target type and a ForeachAIteratorMode option.

touch_points.label: SQL-standard conflict or non-standard syntax
touch_points.reason: FOREACH ... IN ARRAY accepts jsonb with by-name binding and a casting rule that differs from the SQL/JSON lax default.

touch_points.label: maintenance burden ("who maintains this in 10 years")
touch_points.reason: A new iterator contract for every subscriptable type, and casting semantics in PL/pgSQL that cannot change after release.

touch_points.label: doesn't fit what Postgres is about (extension / external tool / already solved)
touch_points.reason: FOR IN SELECT over jsonb_array_elements and FOREACH over an array built once already cover the use case.

questions: Why can coercion not stay in PL/pgSQL, given that message #25 shows the separate coerce callback at about 48 ms against 61 ms for FOR IN SELECT in the int case?
Which ForeachAIteratorMode values does PL/pgSQL use, and which must every type's iterator support?
Which casting default will FOREACH over jsonb keep, and how would a later ERROR ON ERROR clause fit without changing existing functions?
Why should jsonb share the IN ARRAY spelling when it binds object fields by name and rejects SLICE greater than zero?
How does the patch compare with FOREACH over an array built once by array(select jsonb_array_elements...), for scalar and composite targets?

committability.owner_note: Tom Lane is a listed reviewer and commented on the iterator design in message #20, but has not replied to the last two versions. The owner must know PL/pgSQL execution and the subscripting support API.
committability.liability: The owner signs for the iterator contract in SubscriptRoutines that extension types may implement, and for the jsonb casting and by-name binding rules in FOREACH. Both are permanent once released.
committability.author_follow_up: The author posted new versions after each review round and moved the entry to the next CommitFest in October 2026, which suggests he stays for fixes.

priority.reason: The thread names no workload where jsonb loop overhead is the bottleneck, and the gain applies mainly to loops with a pure PL/pgSQL body. The patch is about 40 KiB in pl_exec.c and the subscripting code, and it adds an extension-facing API whose shape a committer questioned without a visible answer.

provisional_note: The code was not read, so the supported iterator modes, the handling of plain json input, and the real cost of moving coercion into PL/pgSQL could not be checked. Only 3 of 28 messages were shown in full; later messages are known through the objections.
disclosure: Prepared by an AI harness; treat as a devil's advocate, not a verdict.

precedents_retrieved.title: iteration over record in plpgsql
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds a row_to_array function that turns any row into a text array of field names and values. It also extends plpgsql FOREACH so a list of target variables, such as key and value, can take consecutive elements of an array in one step.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane objected that row_to_array casts all fields to text and drops SQL datatypes, and said row_to_json already covers the case. He also asked that the two features be split and that FOREACH get its own discussion. Jim Nasby worried that the FOREACH pairing rule would block iteration that follows array dimensions. The later messages move to typed iteration over records and broader dynamic typing, and no revised design was agreed.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
While I don't have a problem with hstore_to_array, I don't think that
row_to_array is a very good idea; it's basically encouraging people to
throw away SQL datatypes altogether and imagine that everything is text.

precedents_retrieved.title: Add jsonb_translate(jsonb, from, to)
precedents_retrieved.objectors: Andrew Dunstan, Pavel Stehule, Peter Eisentraut
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds jsonb_translate(jsonb, from, to), and in v2 json_translate, which recursively replaces every value, including array elements, that exactly equals a given string with another string. The author meant it for mapping categorical or enum values deep inside a document, in the style of the Unix tr utility.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Andrew Dunstan judged blind replacement of every instance of a string, regardless of context, to be a niche use and asked why it could not be an extension. Pavel Stehule suggested using JsonPath to say what to replace, and Peter Eisentraut pointed to json_transform in Oracle and the SQL standard draft, noting that json_transform and json_translate together might confuse users. The thread ends there, and the author later withdrew the entry.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
Blindly replacing every
instance of a single string regardless of context seems at best a niche
use. Is there any reason not to make this an extension?

precedents_retrieved.title: plpgsql - possibility to get element or array type for referenced variable type
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch lets PL/pgSQL `%TYPE` refer to variables of composite type, including polymorphic parameters. It also adds syntax to derive the array type or the element type of a referenced variable, first as `%ARRAYTYPE`/`%ELEMENTTYPE` and later as `%TYPE[]` and `ELEMENT OF ...%TYPE`.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane proposed rejecting this PL/pgSQL-only implementation. He wanted these type operators added to the core grammar's Typename production, so PL/pgSQL would pick them up automatically. Joe Conway and Jim Nasby agreed. The author then found that a reduced patch with only the composite `%TYPE` fix gave too little benefit, and asked for it to be rejected.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
I played with the reduced patch, and the benefit without all other things
is negligible. It should be rejected.

precedents_retrieved.title: Rearrange execution of PARAM_EXTERN Params for plpgsql's benefit.
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Rearrange execution of PARAM_EXTERN Params for plpgsql's benefit.
Reverted commit(s): Further reduce overhead for passing plpgsql variables to the executor.
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This patch does three interrelated things:

* Create a new expression execution step type EEOP_PARAM_CALLBACK
and add the infrastructure needed for add-on modules to generate that.
As discussed, the best control mechanism for that seems to be to add
another hook function to ParamListInfo, which will be called by
ExecInitExpr if it's supplied and a PARAM_EXTERN Param is found.
For stand-alone expressions, we add a new entry point to allow the
ParamListInfo to be specified directly, since it can't be retrieved
from the parent plan node's EState.

* Redesign the API for the ParamListInfo paramFetch hook so that the
ParamExternData array can be entirely virtual.  This also lets us get rid
of ParamListInfo.paramMask, instead leaving it to the paramFetch hook to
decide which param IDs should be accessible or not.  plpgsql_param_fetch
was already doing the identical masking check, so having callers do it too
seemed redundant.  While I was at it, I added a "speculative" flag to
paramFetch that the planner can specify as TRUE to avoid unwanted failures.
This solves an ancient problem for plpgsql that it couldn't provide values
of non-DTYPE_VAR variables to the planner for fear of triggering premature
"record not assigned yet" or "field not found" errors during planning.

* Rework plpgsql to get rid of the need for "unshared" parameter lists,
by dint of turning the single ParamListInfo per estate into a nearly
read-only data structure that doesn't instantiate any per-variable data.
Instead, the paramFetch hook controls access to per-variable data and can
make the right decisions on the fly, replacing the cases that we used to
need multiple ParamListInfos for.  This might perhaps have been a
performance loss on its own, but by using a paramCompile hook we can
bypass plpgsql_param_fetch entirely during normal query execution.
(It's now only called when, eg, we copy the ParamListInfo into a cursor
portal.  copyParamList() or SerializeParamList() effectively instantiate
the virtual parameter array as a simple physical array without a
paramFetch hook, which is what we want in those cases.)  This allows
reverting most of commit 6c82d8d1f, though I kept the cosmetic
code-consolidation aspects of that (eg the assign_simple_var function).

Performance testing shows this to be at worst a break-even change,
and it can provide wins ranging up to 20% in test cases involving
accesses to fields of "record" variables.  The fact that values of
such variables can now be exposed to the planner might produce wins
in some situations, too, but I've not pursued that angle.

In passing, remove the "parent" pointer from the arguments to
ExecInitExprRec and related functions, instead storing that pointer in a
transient field in ExprState.  The ParamListInfo pointer for a stand-alone
expression is handled the same way; we'd otherwise have had to add
yet another recursively-passed-down argument in expression compilation.

precedents_retrieved.title: jsonb array-style subscription
precedents_retrieved.summary: Add array-style subscripting to jsonb, so that values can be read with expressions like test_json['a']['a1'] and updated with assignments like UPDATE ... SET test_json['a']['a1']['a2'] = 42. The work-in-progress patch did this by extending the existing ArrayRef node, using the parser's hard-coded array subscript handling, to cover jsonb.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The visible messages do not show why. The early messages raise design concerns: using array syntax as key/value syntax, update assignments creating missing intermediate objects, and the lack of an operator that could use a GIN index. The visible messages end in August 2015 and the decision was in March 2016, so the shown text does not connect any of these concerns to the outcome.

precedents_retrieved.title: de-TOAST'ing using a iterator
precedents_retrieved.summary: Add an iterator that de-TOASTs and decompresses a toasted value piece by piece, so callers fetch only the part they need. The first user is position(), which can stop early when the match is near the start of the value.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The thread stalled with design problems still open. The iterator structs are exposed in headers, detoast.h ends up including genam.h, and the TOAST code may become heapam-dependent again. John Naylor, who had taken the patch over, said he could not fix the architectural awkwardness and would not work on it in the near future. Anastasia Lubennikova then returned it with feedback.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
For background, this was a 2019 GSoC project where
I was reviewer of record, and the patch is mostly good, but there is some
architectural awkwardness. I have tried to address that, but have not had
success.

precedents_retrieved.title: Iterating on IndexTuple attributes and nbtree page-level dynamic prefix truncation
precedents_retrieved.summary: Patch 0001 adds an API to iterate over index tuple attributes and reuse the offset of the last extracted attribute, so extracting all attributes costs O(n) instead of O(n*n) when attcacheoff cannot be used. Patch 0002 uses this to truncate attribute prefixes dynamically during nbtree binary search within a page, as a first step toward prefix truncation in nbtree.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The author's own June 2021 benchmarks showed regressions in multi-column indexes that can use attcacheoff: about 2% for insert and 15% for reindex with both patches. The author said this had to be fixed before commit, but no fixed version appears in the thread. In December 2021 Daniel Gustafsson moved the entry forward and noted that the patch no longer applied and needed a rebase. The visible messages do not show a rebased version or the final decision.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: Evidently, this needs improvements in the (likely common) attcacheoff-enabled multi-column case; as I don't think we can reasonably commit a 10+% regression.

precedents_retrieved.title: When deleting the plpgsql function, release the CachedPlan of the function
precedents_retrieved.objectors: Matthias van de Meent, Tom Lane
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch frees the CachedPlan contexts of a PL/pgSQL function or procedure when DROP FUNCTION or DROP PROCEDURE runs, so they no longer stay in CacheMemoryContext until the session ends. The author showed with pg_get_backend_memory_contexts() that a dropped and recreated procedure leaves two sets of CachedPlan contexts.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The patch frees cached plans only in the backend that runs the DROP, because other sessions do not execute RemoveFunctionById and keep their plans. Tom Lane suggested that PL/pgSQL, or funccache.c so SQL functions also benefit, install a shared-cache-invalidation callback on pg_proc that marks function trees as deletable. The author agreed, linked a new thread, and withdrew this entry. Vladlen Popolitov also asked why the plans should be freed at all.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: It doesn't, which is (one reason) why it's just a crude hack.

precedents_retrieved.title: When deleting the plpgsql function, release the CachedPlan of the function
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch frees a plpgsql function's compiled parse tree, and the cached plans it links to through SPI, when the function is dropped or invalidated, so the memory is not leaked. A later version registers a syscache callback in cached_function_compile and adds a hash table that maps invalidation hash values to function keys.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The visible messages do not show why. Tom Lane called dropping the function-cache entry a reasonable idea, and the author reported that the new version still emitted duplicate warnings. The last message is a patch update on 2025-09-05 with no reply before the withdrawal.

roaster_notes.note: No precedent gives a rejection reason that still applies. P1's objection was about dropping SQL datatypes through text, and this design keeps target types. P3's objection to a PL/pgSQL-only mechanism was addressed when the patch moved to SubscriptRoutines after messages #11 and #13. P10 records no reason. The open question about target-type knowledge in the iterator (messages #20, #24) belongs to the design angle.
Three objections found within the standards and compatibility angle.

The proposal changes no on-disk format, WAL record, catalog, or wire protocol. Its only cross-boundary surface is an optional field appended to SubscriptRoutines; extensions are rebuilt for each major release, and a NULL field means no iterator, so existing subscript handlers keep working. Whether the iterator API itself is general enough is a design question for another angle.

The proposal has no privilege or exposure aspect worth raising. FOREACH iterates over a jsonb value the function already holds, under the caller's existing privileges, and adds no catalog object, role, GUC or SQL-visible function. The iterator runs inside PL/pgSQL, away from query quals, so leakproofness and RLS are not involved.
